summaries.example: Imagine a mystery club checking a story about what happened at school. One clue says the classroom was empty, another says everyone was inside, and a third explains why the lights were on. A coherence view asks whether the clues fit together and support one another. But a group could also make a different story fit together, so philosophers ask which set of ideas should count.
summaries.summary: The coherence theory of truth says that an idea is true exactly when it coheres with a specified set of other ideas. Coherence might mean consistency, logical support, or a web of mutual explanations. The theory differs from correspondence theory: correspondence says truth depends on matching objective features of the world, while coherence looks to relations among propositions. Coherentists face questions about which set of beliefs should be used and whether truth can go beyond what anyone believes. Critics also ask whether coherence already depends on logic. Some philosophers defend a global theory for all propositions; others consider a partial theory for particular kinds of claims.
key_ideas: The coherence theory says that a proposition is true when it fits with a particular set of propositions.
Different versions disagree about what “fits” means. It might mean not contradicting, logical support, or mutual explanation.
They also disagree about which set matters: what people believe now, what people might believe after careful inquiry, or what an all-knowing being believes.
A major problem is choosing the right set. Many different groups of beliefs might be internally neat.
Another problem asks whether some truths can exist even when no people know or believe them.
Some philosophers suggest coherence may work better for certain subjects, such as mathematics, moral claims, or “what if” claims, than for every kind of statement.
summaries.why_it_matters: This debate helps us understand what we mean when we call something true. It reminds us that a belief can fit nicely with other beliefs and still leave an important question unanswered: are those beliefs connected to the world, or only to one another? Thinking about this can make us more careful when comparing stories, explanations, and evidence.

important_terms.definition: A statement or idea that can be judged true or false.
A way of saying that something is true when it fits with and is supported by a chosen group of other ideas.
The connection between ideas when they fit together without clashing and help explain one another.
The idea that a statement is true when it matches how things really are in the world.
A group of statements or beliefs used to check whether another statement fits.

questions_to_think_about: Can a story be neat and well-supported but still be wrong?
How would you choose the right group of beliefs for testing an idea?
Could something be true even if nobody ever discovers it?
Is fitting with other ideas enough, or should we also check the world?

summaries.example: Suppose a student builds a theory that a school’s power failed because of a storm. The theory fits reports of dark classrooms, a weather record, and a damaged line. A different theory might fit a smaller collection of reports just as well. A correspondence theorist asks which theory matches the actual event. A coherentist instead explains truth through a specified system of propositions and must say why one system, rather than another, is the relevant one.
summaries.summary: Coherentism identifies truth with coherence: a proposition is true if and only if it fits a specified system of propositions. The theory leaves open several choices. Coherence may be consistency, entailment, or mutual explanatory support; the system may consist of actual beliefs, beliefs reached at an ideal limit of inquiry, or the beliefs of an omniscient being. Its main competitors and criticisms concern the role of objective reality. Correspondence theory makes objective conditions the truth conditions, whereas coherentism treats other propositions as truth conditions. Critics raise specification, transcendence, and logic objections. Defenders argue that some objections assume correspondence or an independent standard before proving it. Recent proposals also distinguish global coherentism from partial coherentism, which applies only to selected classes of propositions.
key_ideas: Coherence theories are substantive theories of truth: they try to explain truth through truth conditions and relations among propositions, rather than merely repeating that a proposition is true.
Versions differ over whether coherence is consistency, entailment, or reciprocal explanatory support, and over who supplies the specified beliefs.

A coherence theory based on beliefs held by actual or finite inquirers tends to reject realism about truth, especially bivalence and transcendence. A theory based on an omniscient being avoids some of that pressure.

The specification objection argues that coherentists lack a non-question-begging way to identify the relevant system. The fact that a system is large, simple, or empirically adequate may not uniquely select one.
The transcendence objection says that some propositions may be true even though they never cohere with any humanly available system. Coherentists reply that this assumes what they deny.
The logic objection says that coherence seems to presuppose rules such as non-contradiction. Coherentists answer that such rules can themselves belong to, and support, a coherent system.
summaries.why_it_matters: The issue affects how we understand inquiry, evidence, and disagreement. If truth is coherence, careful reasoning may require examining an entire network of commitments rather than testing isolated statements. Yet the theory must explain why one network is authoritative and whether truth can outrun what thinkers can establish. Those questions connect theories of truth with theories of justification and with debates about science, morality, mathematics, and counterfactual claims.

important_terms.definition: A truth-bearer: here, a statement or idea that can have a truth value, true or false.
The view that a proposition is true if and only if it coheres with a specified set of propositions.
A relation such as consistency, entailment, or mutual explanatory support among propositions.
The view that a proposition is true when its truth conditions are objective features of the world that it matches.
The conditions that must obtain for a proposition to be true. Coherence theories treat these conditions as involving propositions in a system.
The chosen system of propositions with which a proposition must cohere for the theory to call it true.
The claim that every proposition is either true or false.
The claim that a proposition can be true even if it cannot be known to be true.

questions_to_think_about: If two belief systems are equally consistent and equally large, what could make one the specified set?
Does the fact that we can know only that a proposition coheres show that truth itself is coherence?
Can a proposition be true if no finite community could ever settle it?
Does a theory of truth need to explain how beliefs connect with an objective world?
Would coherence be more plausible for moral or mathematical claims than for ordinary scientific claims?

summaries.example: Your class is trying to decide whether a rumor about a canceled game is true. One group of messages says the field is flooded, the coach announced a cancellation, and several students saw the notice. Those messages support one another. But another group of messages might also fit together, perhaps because everyone repeated the same mistake. A coherence theorist must explain which group is the relevant set and what makes the messages cohere.
summaries.summary: The coherence theory says that a proposition is true just when it coheres with a specified set of propositions. Philosophers disagree about the relation involved: consistency, logical support, or mutual explanation. They also disagree about the set itself, which could be formed from present beliefs, ideal inquiry, or an omniscient perspective. This creates a central difficulty: if several systems fit together, how can the theory select the right one without appealing to correspondence with facts? Another challenge is that some truths may be beyond anything finite thinkers believe. The article also compares coherentism with correspondence theory and considers whether coherentism should apply to all propositions or only to areas such as ethics, mathematics, and counterfactuals.
key_ideas: Coherentists say truth depends on how propositions relate to a specified set, not directly on a match with non-propositional facts.
Some versions define coherence as consistency. Others use entailment or mutual explanatory support because mere consistency can allow two incompatible claims to fit the same set.
The specified set might be actual human beliefs, beliefs reached by people like us after inquiry, or the beliefs of an omniscient being.
The specification objection asks how a coherentist can identify the correct set without quietly using facts or standards from a competing theory.

The transcendence objection asks whether a claim can be true even when it lies beyond every human system of beliefs. The coherentist may reply that this challenge assumes an independent kind of truth.
Arguments for coherentism have come from metaphysical views associated with idealism and from epistemological concerns about how we test and justify beliefs.
summaries.why_it_matters: The theory shows that truth and justification are related but not automatically identical. A belief system can be organized, consistent, and persuasive, yet philosophers still ask whether it captures reality. Studying the dispute helps us evaluate evidence without confusing agreement or internal logic with a final answer about the world.

important_terms.definition: A statement or idea that can be true or false.
The theory that a proposition is true when it fits with a chosen group of other propositions.
A relationship in which ideas do not conflict and may support or explain one another.
The theory that truth means matching facts or conditions in the world.
A group of propositions used as the standard for deciding whether another proposition coheres.
A relation in which some propositions support or imply another proposition.
The view that a claim can be true even if no one can know that it is true.

questions_to_think_about: Why is simple consistency not enough to show that a claim is true?
Could two different systems of beliefs each be equally coherent?
Does being unable to check a claim against reality prove that it is not correspondence-true?
What might be gained by treating moral claims as parts of a coherent system?
Should a truth theory explain what makes claims true, how we recognize truth, or both?
